**FCA signals open banking data will reshape mortgage affordability checks**

*The FCA has outlined plans to use open banking and open finance data to broaden mortgage access, moving beyond traditional income evidence towards real-time transaction-based assessments.*

The FCA published a blog post by Emad Aladhal setting out how the regulator intends to modernise mortgage affordability rules to reflect how people actually earn and spend today. The proposal centres on enabling lenders to use open banking data, such as transaction histories and real-time income verification, to assess borrowers who are currently underserved by conventional documentation requirements. Self-employed workers, gig economy participants and those with non-standard income patterns are the clearest beneficiaries.

This is not a new regulatory consultation but a public statement of direction from within the FCA, and it matters because it represents one of the most concrete use cases the regulator has endorsed for open finance beyond payments. The UK's open banking infrastructure has largely been discussed in terms of payment initiation and account aggregation; the FCA is now explicitly pointing lenders towards using shared financial data to make credit decisions differently.

For mortgage lenders and open banking providers alike, the signal is clear: the FCA expects the market to move towards data-driven affordability. Firms building credit decisioning or income verification tools on open banking rails have a regulatory tailwind, while lenders that continue to rely solely on payslips and bank statements risk falling behind both competitors and supervisory expectations.

*Sources: [Opening the door to mortgages: rules focused on better outcomes for people](https://www.fca.org.uk/news/blogs/opening-door-mortgages-rules-focused-better-outcomes-people) — FCA*

**Lloyds Banking Group deploys agentic AI for real-time scam detection**

*Lloyds is using agentic AI to screen payments for fraud in real time across its 28 million customer base, one of the first large-scale deployments of autonomous AI agents in UK banking fraud prevention.*

Lloyds Banking Group has expanded its fraud prevention systems to include agentic AI capable of independently checking payments for scam indicators as they are initiated. The system operates in real time, adding an autonomous decision layer to the bank's existing fraud controls. It covers Lloyds' full retail and business customer base of 28 million accounts.

The deployment is notable for its scale and its use of agentic rather than conventional rule-based or supervised machine learning approaches. Agentic AI systems can reason across multiple data points and take actions without waiting for human intervention at each step, which is particularly relevant for the speed requirements of instant payments fraud screening. UK banks have been under increasing pressure since the Payment Systems Regulator's mandatory reimbursement rules took effect, creating a direct financial incentive to stop scams before money leaves accounts rather than compensating victims afterwards.

Lloyds is not the first UK bank to invest heavily in AI-powered fraud detection, but the explicit use of agentic architecture at this scale across a major high-street bank suggests the technology is moving from pilot to production. For other banks and payment providers, it sets a benchmark for what regulators and customers may come to expect.

*Sources: [Lloyds deploys AI agents to check for payment scams in real-time](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/47884/lloyds-deploys-ai-agents-to-check-for-payment-scams-in-real-time) — Finextra*

**TrueLayer launches bank-on-file to challenge card-on-file at checkout**

*TrueLayer's new product stores bank account details for repeat purchases, directly targeting the card networks' grip on recurring ecommerce payments.*

TrueLayer launched a product called "Bank on File" at Money20/20, designed to let consumers save their bank account as a stored payment method with online merchants, mirroring the card-on-file model that underpins much of ecommerce today. The aim is to make account-to-account payments as frictionless for repeat purchases as stored card credentials, removing the main UX barrier that has limited pay-by-bank adoption in online retail.

The structural challenge for account-to-account payments in ecommerce has always been the authentication step. Card-on-file lets returning customers pay in one click; open banking payments have typically required re-authentication with the bank each time. By storing a tokenised bank account reference, TrueLayer is attempting to close that gap. If it works at scale, it could shift the competitive dynamics between account-to-account and card rails for subscription and repeat-purchase merchants.

The timing is deliberate. With PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation nearing adoption, and Wero expanding across European markets, the infrastructure and regulatory conditions for stored account-to-account payments are converging. TrueLayer is betting that the open banking ecosystem is mature enough to support persistent payment relationships, not just one-off transfers.

*Sources: [TrueLayer Launches 'Bank on File' at Money20/20 to Direct-Challenge Card Dominance](https://thefintechtimes.com/truelayer-launches-bank-on-file-at-money20-20-to-direct-challenge-card-dominance/) — The Fintech Times*

**ClearBank positions for eurozone instant payments growth**

*ClearBank is expanding its eurozone instant payments capability, betting that the EU's mandatory instant payments regulation will drive demand for cloud-native clearing infrastructure.*

ClearBank has signalled its intent to build around projected growth in eurozone instant payments, with its European CEO outlining the firm's positioning as the regulation mandating full SEPA instant credit transfer availability takes effect. The UK-headquartered clearing bank, which holds a euro banking licence, is targeting fintechs and payment firms that need access to instant euro clearing without building direct connections to legacy infrastructure.

The opportunity is structural. The EU's instant payments regulation requires all euro-area payment service providers to be able to send and receive instant credit transfers at no premium to standard transfers. Many smaller banks and non-bank payment institutions lack the technical readiness to meet these requirements and will need to access instant payment rails through intermediaries. ClearBank's cloud-native model, already proven in the UK's Faster Payments ecosystem, is designed for exactly this kind of agency clearing.

For the broader market, ClearBank's move illustrates how the instant payments regulation is creating commercial opportunities not just for banks themselves but for the infrastructure providers that sit behind them. The eurozone instant payments market is expected to grow rapidly as the regulatory deadline approaches, and the competition to provide clearing-as-a-service is intensifying.

*Sources: [ClearBank Positions Around Projected Growth in Eurozone Instant Payments](https://www.tipranks.com/news/private-companies/clearbank-positions-around-projected-growth-in-eurozone-instant-payments) — TipRanks*

**FDATA proposes tiered model to keep smaller fintechs in Canadian open banking**

*FDATA has put forward a tiered accreditation framework for Canada's open banking regime, drawing on the UK's FCA agent model to prevent compliance costs from shutting out smaller participants.*

The Financial Data and Technology Association has proposed a model for Canada's emerging open banking framework that would allow smaller fintechs to participate through a tiered or agent-based accreditation structure rather than meeting the full compliance burden independently. The proposal explicitly references the UK's FCA-authorised agent model and Australia's Consumer Data Right framework as precedents.

The concern is straightforward: if open banking accreditation requires the same compliance investment from a five-person fintech as from a major bank, smaller firms will be excluded from the ecosystem. This has been a recurring tension in every jurisdiction that has implemented open banking. In the UK, the agent model allowed smaller third-party providers to operate under the regulatory umbrella of a larger authorised firm, lowering the barrier to entry while maintaining supervisory standards.

Canada is at a formative stage with its open banking legislation. FDATA's intervention is an attempt to shape the rules before they are set, and the outcome will determine whether Canada's framework produces a competitive, diverse ecosystem or concentrates data access among a small number of large players. For European observers, it is a useful reference point for how the same design questions are being addressed in PSD3 and the Financial Data Access regulation.

*Sources: [FDATA proposes model to ensure smaller fintechs can participate in Open Banking in Canada](https://www.openbankingexpo.com/news/fdata-proposes-fintech-model-to-ensure-smaller-players-can-participate-in-open-banking-in-canada/) — Open Banking Expo*
